source.version_note: Scientific Reports9:13080,2019. Supplied first page has publication-date placeholder; Crossref identifies publication11September2019. Seven human studies,not an autonomous-vehicle implementation.

citation.title: Human decision-making biases in the moral dilemmas of autonomous vehicles

reading.source_scope_note: Human hypothetical crash choices under time/perspective/visual manipulations. No deployed AI model,actual collision,perceived-agency mediator or uniquely identified intuitive/deliberative process is measured.
access_limits: All19extracted pages read,including participant exclusions,pooled regressions,Study7repeated-trial protocol,internal meta-analysis,limitations and references. Rendered pages10and14inspected for seating cues and the10752-observation regression.

External supplement,raw data,regression code,cutoff/pilot analyses and any preregistration were not independently opened or reproduced. Cited Kahneman,Simon,Bandura and other original sources/books remain unread.

study.online_tasks: One crash choice per person; Studies1–4assigned5sversus30sinstructions,then exclude intuitive responses≥7sand deliberate responses<7s;5/6no mode manipulation
study.study_2: Reverses which path kills which role; pooled withStudy1,N1212,default-path OR.87,CI[.66,1.16],p.346
study.study_4: Replaces added adult with child; pooled withStudy3,N594,reportedOR1.06,CI[.94,1.20],p.333;contrast coding needsclarification
study.study_5: Randomized3roles x2seat positions; no time exclusions; rear-seat pedestrian-sacrificeOR2.23,CI[1.24,4.03],p.007
study.study_6: Randomized3roles x3norm displays; ambiguous red-light high-violationOR.61,CI[.37,.99],p.047,opposite hypothesis

study_7.design: Time condition between-person;3roles x28fractional-factorial scenarios within-person;observeralwaysfirst

study.meta_analysis: Single-paper synthesis ofStudies1–6,reuses their data;reportedI²69.9%,CI[54.75,79.98],not independent confirmation

summary: Add agency attribution bias as the authors' named interpretation of a seat-cue effect,with the unmeasured-mediator limit explicit. Enrich perspective taking and dual-process evidence without treating imagined roles as accurate empathy or time pressure as a unique cognitive mechanism. Retain noncorroborating default/action tests and major repeated-observation/selection limits.

findings.definition: Inferring an actor's control over an outcome from agency-related cues that do not change the actor's actual control.
findings.ai_evidence_status: Author-proposed interpretation of a randomized human seating-cue effect; perceived agency itself is not directly measured and no AI inference task is tested
findings.ai_proposal: Present an AI with matched cases where an occupant's visual position or title suggests control but actual decision authority is explicitly unchanged. Check whether it assigns control,responsibility or blame from the cue instead of the stated causal role. Separately test the proposed mediator rather than inferring it from a verdict change.
findings.novelty_rationale: Attribution of another actor's agency differs from one's own sense/illusion of control and from explaining behavior by disposition rather than circumstances. The paper names Agency Bias and specifies a control-constant seating comparison; retain one entry and alias,not duplicate mechanisms.

evidence.quote: people’s attribution of agency could bias their moral decision
the passenger’s agency is the same

findings.evidence_scope: Study5N302randomized front/back seat and imagined role. Rear-seat condition increases hypothetical pedestrian sacrifice relative to front-seat,OR2.23,p.007. The described vehicle is fully autonomous in both cases. Agency/responsibility and alternative seat associations are not separately measured;the mechanism is proposed,not identified.
findings.boundary: A position cue can legitimately indicate control in other contexts;the bias concerns inference beyond actual authority in a matched case. The result is a human choice effect,not proof of felt agency,an autonomous car's blameworthiness or a demonstrated model defect. Seating can also change salience,assumed risk or learned role associations.

findings.term: Imagined role changes hypothetical moral choices
findings.definition: Asking people to imagine being a passenger,pedestrian or observer changes which side they tend to preserve in fixed crash scenarios.
findings.novelty_rationale: Adds a second fully read source using an explicit imagined-role manipulation to the existing perspective-taking entry,not a duplicate generic personal-bias label.

evidence.quote: Imagine that you are the [passenger of the car;

findings.evidence_scope: Online single-choice studies and Danish repeated-choice lab study use role instructions. The lab passenger/pedestrian contrast is reported with many repeated trials and no specified participant-level adjustment;source uncertainty remains.
findings.boundary: Imagining a role need not produce accurate understanding,shared feelings,altruism or impartiality. Personal stakes are materially salient,so changed preferences are not automatically irrational. The observer condition is not a proven neutral gold standard.

findings.term: Time pressure is a manipulation,not a direct readout of moral-processing systems
findings.definition: Faster instructed decision conditions show lower rates of choosing pedestrian sacrifice in these tasks;the authors interpret this through a dual-process account.
findings.novelty_rationale: Relevant experimental evidence for the existing theory's behavioral predictions,with explicit limits on causal process identification.

evidence.quote: Time pressure was used to trigger intuitive decisions

findings.evidence_scope: Studies1–4postselect responses around7sunder5/30sinstructions;Study7uses enforced5/60slimits,repeats missed trials and gives different training. No direct emotion,working-memory or intuitive-processing measure establishes a unique system.
findings.boundary: A time limit can affect attention,reading,stress,response strategy and comprehension. Sacrificing a passenger is not universally deontological,especially in equal-casualty or changed-default cases. Fast answers need not be emotional and slower answers need not be more rational.

findings.term: No detected default-path effect is not absence of status-quo bias everywhere
findings.definition: Changing the vehicle's default path does not produce a detected source effect in the reported online pooled test or lab test,but neither test establishes general equivalence.
findings.novelty_rationale: A noncorroborating/control finding under the existing default preference entry,not a supporting positive-effect paper used to fill a bibliography gap.
findings.evidence_scope: Studies1/2are separate recruitment samples with reversed routes;labdefaultOR1.08,CI[.99,1.18],p.095uses repeated trial rows.
findings.boundary: A nonsignificant contrast does not rule out meaningful effects,prove unbiased preferences or validate every alternative moral explanation. Route changes also alter causal roles;status quo and omission are not the same construct.

findings.term: Action versus inaction explanation remains a tested alternative,not confirmed bias
findings.definition: The researchers test whether a preference to change course explains passenger sacrifice;the main reversed-path contrast does not support that account in this setup.
findings.novelty_rationale: Retains a useful negative test under the existing action-bias record without inventing a new mechanism or claiming all alternatives are excluded.

evidence.quote: action (changing the path of the vehicle) over inaction

findings.evidence_scope: Action/default explanation compared by separate one-versus-one crash versions. No positive action-bias effect is established.
findings.boundary: Choosing either option can be morally relevant given intentions and consequences. No detected change is not proof that the remaining preference is uniquely unbiased or that action/inaction matters nowhere.

methodological_limits: The paper concerns human choices about fixed hypothetical crashes,not an autonomous system learning or executing a moral policy. Its background assertion that MoralMachine-derived algorithms are deployed in AVs is not demonstrated by these studies.

OnlineStudies1–4allow time limits to be exceeded,then remove slow intuitive and fast deliberate responses using a7scutoff. That is post-treatment selection on a variable related to the outcome,not an unqualified intention-to-treat estimate of randomized time instructions.

Study1excludes198/807,Study2retains603/848,Study3retains286/393andStudy4retains308/428. Cutoff justification includes correspondence/floodlight analysis on response patterns;external specification and sensitivity analyses were not read.

Time pressure does not isolate a cognitive system. It changes opportunity to read,stress,heuristics and strategy,and no direct emotion/working-memory measure establishes the claimed emotional-versus-rational mechanism.

Study7has128people x84choices=10752rows. The reported ordinary binary logistic model lists10752observations and no participant/stimulus clustering,mixed effects or covariance adjustment. Repeated observations need appropriate dependence handling;raw code is required to assess uncertainty.

Person-level predictors in the10752-row model,including age,license and time condition,do not have10752independent participants. Their narrow intervals should not be treated as independent-person precision.

Observer perspective is alwaysfirst in the lab,while the two personal-role blocks are later and randomized with each other. Observer-versus-personal contrasts are confounded with block order,fatigue and learning;one presentation-order covariate cannot by itself remove that fixed confound.

The fast lab group receives six circle-comparison training trials whereas the deliberate group does not. Grouped session batches and different session duration can add training/session differences to the time manipulation.

Missed lab trials recur until a response is recorded. Re-exposure permits learning and advance consideration and can change an ostensible first intuitive decision;number of repeats by condition is not fully reported here.

Study5randomizes seat position but does not measure inferred agency,blame or perceived control. A seating-cue effect is consistent with the proposed agency account but also salience,risk assumptions and learned role associations.

No actual change of passenger control occurs,but making a scene visually similar to a driver need not alter every respondent's agency belief. The claim that the mechanism is confirmed overstates the available mediator evidence.

Personal-role instructions change self-relevance and stakes in the imagined situation. Concern for one's own survival is not inherently a reasoning error;the paper's unbiased observer baseline is assumed rather than independently validated.

One-versus-one choices cannot identify casualty-maximizing utilitarianism. The paper acknowledges this early,but later generalizes sacrificing passengers as deontological across conditions. Ethical doctrines are not uniquely diagnosed by which side dies.
More saved lives,younger victims,traffic law and action/inaction are different dimensions. Majority choices do not authorize ranking lives or using fatalities as punishment for jaywalking.

OnlineStudy4does not detect a child-passenger effect,whereas labStudy7does. Describing the lab child result as in line withStudy4suppresses the earlier null;the tasks,populations and dependence structures differ.

Study6norm effect is opposite prediction. The authors plausibly attribute it to an ambiguous red light and redesign the lab display,but they do not directly measure the original participants' signal interpretation. Revised stimuli plus different sample/design do not isolate that explanation.

Low/high norm displays change road markings,lights and scene complexity,not just moral lawfulness. Pedestrian legality,causal responsibility,attention and visual interpretation are not cleanly separated.
Null default-path tests do not establish exact invariance,absence of action/status-quo bias or unbiased moral preferences. No equivalence margin is specified.
Study1body gives ageOR.78,CI[.44,.94],while Table1gives[.65,.94]. Table1/5also label age inyears despite ORs around.7perunit;exact coding/scaling should be checked before quantitative interpretation.

The pooled child contrast OR1.06,CI[.94,1.20]is reported as a binary child-versus-adult condition comparison,but its units/coding are not documented sufficiently to reconcile the narrow interval with this sample/design. No correction is guessed.

Several results passages refer to Table2for regressions that are actually in Table1;Table2is a percentage table. Preserve correct source locators and do not infer new datasets from repeated pooled models.
Pooled rowsN1212,889,594reuse adjacent studies rather than independent new participants. The distinct analyzed people total2844(including128lab),not the sum of all pooled regression observations.

The internal meta-analysis reusesStudies1–6and reports high heterogeneity,I²69.9%. It is useful within-paper synthesis,not independent replication or proof that every scenario follows a universal effect.

Response time as a covariate inStudies5/6is observational and can be influenced by decision difficulty or treatment. It cannot by itself control or identify an experimentally assigned intuitive/deliberative mode.

USonlineworkers and young Danishlab volunteers are not representative US/Western/cross-cultural populations. Extrapolation to representative samples overrepresenting a passenger viewpoint remains a hypothesis.

Study7begins with218prequestionnaire respondents but128attend the lab;selection between stages can limit generality. No independent test shows willingness to attend is unrelated to relevant attitudes.

Deterministic deaths,constrained two-option cartoon scenes and familiarization omit uncertainty,braking,prevention,injury severity and real-world authority. Public approval is not a validated safety/legal objective.

The recommended forcing of respondents into a decision mode can intentionally steer results;the paper itself notes strategic use. That is a governance concern requiring transparent protocol,not evidence one timed preference is morally authoritative.
External supplements,raw data,preregistration and cited books were not read. No source is judged by coauthorship alone,and no unverified misconduct or correction status is asserted.

cross_paper_learning.finding: Martin distinguishes access to passenger/pedestrian perspectives from equal-role lotteries. Frank tests instructed personal roles without a veil lottery;neither imagined perspective nor an observer instruction guarantees impartiality.

As in the euthanasia study,decision patterns cannot be universally labeled deontological/utilitarian from action labels or casualty numbers. Repeated ratings require a documented within-person analysis.

Clearer or richer stimuli may change interpretation without demonstrating objective ethical validity. Selecting responses by an outcome-related proxy and using shared trials as independent units can affect estimates.

deferred.reason: The role effect is documented under perspective taking. A broader general bias term and its normative error criterion need a primary conceptual treatment;do not duplicate a manipulated-role finding under several names.
A descriptive age-related preference is discussed,but its mechanism and normative legitimacy are not established. It is not automatically a new cognitive failure or a valid AI safety policy.
Traffic-legality effects can reflect responsibility,rights or scene interpretation. No specific general punishment mechanism is isolated.
An overarching theoretical framework,not a single newly observed behavior or an additional mechanism demonstrated by these task effects.

limitations: One author-proposed agency-attribution construct is added with process limits explicit. Experimental human choices are not model internals,actual agency or a normative crash policy. Multiple studies,pooled models and within-paper synthesis are not multiple independent research papers.
